h1: Aviation Liquid Penetrant Testing for Aerospace Parts in the US
html:
Atlantis NDT performs aviation liquid penetrant testing (PT, also called dye penetrant or fluorescent penetrant inspection) on metallic aerospace parts in the United States: aluminum, titanium and nickel castings, forgings and machined fittings, welds on tooling and ground support equipment, and structural hardware. Our technicians come to your plant or hangar and apply your own specification and flow-down. To get started, request a PT inspection quote with the part list and the controlling process document.

What penetrant inspection does for aerospace metal

Penetrant testing finds cracks, laps, seams, porosity and shrinkage that break the surface of a non-porous part. It works on aluminum, magnesium, titanium, stainless steel and nickel alloys, all of which resist a magnet, which is why PT carries so much of the aerospace surface-inspection load. A fluorescent penetrant under ultraviolet light reveals a crack only a few ten-thousandths of an inch wide, so it is a standard final check on machined and cast parts before assembly.

The method cannot find flaws below the surface, and it cannot find a crack that has been closed by smeared metal, peening or a coating. For internal flaws in forgings and plate, the right tool is ultrasonic testing; for cracks in ferromagnetic steel, magnetic particle inspection is often more sensitive and less sensitive to surface condition.

Standards, specifications and who signs off

Process requirements for aerospace penetrant work come from the purchase order or the customer's process control document. Those documents normally cite ASTM E1417 for the penetrant practice, which defines the types, methods and sensitivity levels, and ASTM E165 as the general practice, with ASME Section V, Article 6 as a widely recognized method reference. Maintenance and alteration of US-registered aircraft fall under 14 CFR Part 43, and repair stations operate under 14 CFR Part 145. Those certificated persons and stations return aircraft to service. Airworthiness sign-off is not something Atlantis does; our report is data for the customer's quality system.

Atlantis technicians work under the company written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A and aligned to the customer's flow-down. A Level II performs and interprets the examination; an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. The employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A, so tell us if your quality system adds qualification steps for the examiner.

Penetrant types, methods and sensitivity

ASTM E1417 describes Type I fluorescent and Type II visible-dye penetrants. Four methods cover water-washable, lipophilic post-emulsifiable, solvent-removable and hydrophilic post-emulsifiable processes, and five sensitivity levels run from very low to ultra-high. Most aerospace manufacturing work on precision parts uses a fluorescent system in a darkened area, with a sensitivity level set by the specification. Field and shop-floor work on tooling, equipment and large weldments more often uses a visible, solvent-removable kit because it needs no water, no darkness and no power.

A developer pulls the retained penetrant out of the flaw. Dry powder developers suit fluorescent work on smooth, machined surfaces, and nonaqueous wet developers suit visible work. The process specification names the combination, the dwell time for the material and flaw type, and the interval allowed for development before the final reading.

Cleaning, etching and the smeared-metal problem

Surface preparation decides whether PT works at all. Machining, grinding, blasting and peening on soft metals such as aluminum can smear metal across the mouth of a crack and seal it, so the specification may require an etch before penetrant to open the surface. Oil, hydraulic fluid, anodize or conversion coating, paint and carbon deposits all block entry. The cleaning method must remove contaminants without harming the part, so solvents, alkaline cleaners and etchants are chosen for the alloy. After examination, penetrant and developer are removed in a way that protects the finish and leaves nothing in holes, threads or passages.

Titanium and nickel alloys call for penetrant materials controlled for halogen and sulfur content, because residues can attack these alloys at high temperature. Lot numbers for each penetrant material go on the report, as ASTM E165 expects. Our technicians keep clean cloths and brushes for each alloy family, since iron picked up from carbon steel tools can contaminate aluminum and stainless surfaces.

Castings, forgings and welds

Aluminum and magnesium castings can show shrinkage porosity and cold shuts; titanium and nickel investment castings show surface porosity and hot tears. PT is the standard surface method for them, and the acceptance classes in the customer specification tie the permitted indication size and count to the part's criticality. See our penetrant testing of castings page for the technique. Forgings can have laps and seams that show as continuous lines. Welds on structural parts, tooling and equipment are examined for cracks at the toe, crater and root; the penetrant testing of welds page covers that method in detail.

Ground support equipment and tooling often combine steel and aluminum. A stand with welded aluminum legs and steel fittings needs PT on the aluminum and MT or PT on the steel. The owner's engineer decides the rating and the repair, based on our findings.

Process control and what the technician checks

  • Temperature: the part and the penetrant must be inside the specification's range, usually near room temperature; a cold hangar or a hot ramp can fall outside it.
  • Dwell: the penetrant stays wet on the surface for the time listed for the alloy and the flaw type; a dried penetrant must be removed and the process repeated.
  • Removal: too little removal leaves background that hides indications; too much washes the penetrant out of the flaw. The technician checks under light during the process.
  • Lighting: ultraviolet intensity at the part surface and ambient white light are measured against the specification's limits with calibrated meters.
  • System check: a known cracked panel or comparator confirms the system is working, and penetrant condition checks are logged.

Planning around plant and maintenance schedules

Penetrant work generates waste and vapor, and that shapes the plan. The process needs a sink or wipe-down area, ventilation, flammable-liquid handling, waste containers for used materials and, for fluorescent work, a darkened booth or room. Many plants have these in a controlled processing area; for others, we bring a portable kit. Access, badging, safety orientation and export-control briefings may all be required before our technicians start. Parts may be on hold or under quarantine until the report is released, so tell us the date the report is needed and the order in which parts should be examined.

Timing in the process flow matters. PT normally follows final machining and any etch, and precedes conversion coating, anodize and paint, because those finishes can hide cracks. The examination of a finished surface may still be requested, but the report then states the coating condition so the customer can weigh the sensitivity.

Reading and recording indications

Fluorescent indications are read in a darkened area after the technician's eyes adapt, normally with a short pause before the examination starts. Wearing photochromic lenses or lenses that block part of the spectrum can hide faint indications, so the written practice says what eyewear is allowed. A linear indication is one whose length is at least three times its width, and acceptance classes usually treat linear and rounded indications differently. Porosity in a casting may be allowed up to a stated size and spacing, while any crack is rejected regardless of size.

When an indication is questioned, the technician removes it with solvent, cleans the area, reapplies penetrant and developer and reads again, as the specification allows. Photographs with a scale go into the record. Where the specification demands retention of the result, the report carries the images in the same file as the examination data, so the evidence stays with the part history.

What the report contains

The report names the customer and identifies each part by number, serial or lot and drawing revision, with the alloy and condition. It lists the controlling specification and revision, the written procedure, the penetrant system with type, method and sensitivity level, the manufacturer and lot numbers, the cleaning and etch steps, the temperatures, dwell and development times, and the light readings. Each indication is described by location, shape and size, with a photograph or sketch and an accept or reject decision against the stated class. The technician, level and ASNT Level III reviewer are named, and any surface not examined is listed.

What to send for a quote

  • Part numbers, alloys, quantities and surface condition
  • The specification, revision, penetrant system and acceptance class
  • Whether the plant provides a booth, sink, ventilation and waste handling
  • Site location, badging and export-control or safety requirements
  • Report date and any hold or quarantine arrangements

Where we work in the US aerospace market

We mobilize to plants and maintenance sites in these regions. Each page covers PT for that market.

  • Wichita: airframe and business-jet suppliers with many aluminum and titanium parts.
  • Seattle: structures and machining suppliers around Puget Sound.
  • Hartford: engine, rotating part and precision casting work.
  • Charleston: aerostructure assembly and fabrication suppliers.
  • Savannah: business aircraft production and support.
  • Fort Worth: military aircraft and rotorcraft suppliers.
  • Huntsville: launch hardware, missile and space structure fabrication.
  • Phoenix: Arizona aerospace manufacturing and maintenance operations.

Training your own technicians

If your plant wants its own penetrant inspectors, Atlantis offers PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with the penetrant testing simulator. Procedure help is available through procedure qualification and demonstration. The employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A. See aviation NDT training and the national penetrant testing page for more.

What we do not do here

Radiography is not offered by Atlantis in the United States. We do not examine composite or bonded structure, we do not offer specialist techniques on this page, and we do not release aircraft to service. Where your specification names a process approval or examiner qualification that Atlantis does not hold, we say so before scheduling the work.

faq.q: What is aviation liquid penetrant testing used for?
faq.a: It finds surface-breaking cracks, laps, seams and porosity in non-porous aerospace parts such as aluminum, titanium and nickel castings, forgings, machined fittings and welds on tooling and ground support equipment.

faq.q: Can you do fluorescent penetrant inspection at our plant?
faq.a: Yes, when the area can be darkened and the specification's lighting limits are met. The plant either supplies a booth and processing area or we bring portable equipment, which we confirm during scoping.

faq.q: Which penetrant specification will you follow?
faq.a: The one in your purchase order or process document. It usually cites ASTM E1417 and sets the type, method, sensitivity level and acceptance class. We follow those and record the materials and lot numbers on the report.

faq.q: Do you sign off airworthiness after penetrant inspection?
faq.a: No. Airworthiness sign-off is not something Atlantis does. Under 14 CFR Parts 43 and 145 the decision rests with the certificated person or repair station, who uses our report as one input.

faq.q: Why must aluminum parts sometimes be etched before PT?
faq.a: Machining or blasting can smear soft aluminum over a crack and seal it. An etch removes the smeared layer and reopens the flaw, so penetrant can enter. The specification states when it is required.

faq.q: Can PT be done after anodizing or painting?
faq.a: It can be, but coatings can hide fine cracks, so sensitivity drops. Most specifications call for PT before the finish. If a coated surface must be examined, the report records the coating condition.

faq.q: Is penetrant testing better than magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: On nonmagnetic metals it is the surface method. On magnetic steel, MT is often more sensitive and faster, and it also finds near-surface flaws. The specification and part material decide.

faq.q: What do you need to quote penetrant work?
faq.a: A part list with alloys and quantities, the specification and acceptance class, details of the facility such as booth and waste handling, site access and security requirements, and the date the report is needed.

faq.q: Can you examine castings for porosity?
faq.a: We examine them for surface-breaking porosity, shrinkage, hot tears and cold shuts and record them against the casting acceptance class. Internal porosity is outside what PT can find.
